note: Which ICS3U activity pages reach which AP Computer Science Principles learning objectives, for the marketing working folder (~/Plantoir Marketing) only — never the shipped ICS3U payload. marketing_folder.py appends one embed per code (![[CRD-2.I]]) inside each page's existing '## Curriculum connection' block, after the Ontario embeds, so the College Board map counts the page exactly as the Ontario map does. Drafted 2026-09-26 from the website plan's skill-keyed table and RE-KEYED to learning objectives (ruling Q1); every row was checked against the page's full text by three independent Opus readers, and 'evidence' quotes the ICS3U page (our words, not the College Board's). A row nobody could defend from the page was dropped, not softened; they are listed under 'dropped' so they are not proposed again. The reasons are in our own words.

rows.reason: Students combine conditions with and/or/not using a truth table, store a comparison's True/False result in a variable, and see that a negated compound condition can be rewritten as an equivalent one.
rows.evidence: Conditions that combine deserve an operator, not a staircase.

rows.reason: Students question how much personal data their own program stores, look for rules and biases a program quietly builds in, and weigh computing's harms against the good it does.
rows.evidence: A face-recognition system that works less well on some faces than others is a design decision showing up as a failure rate

rows.reason: Students weigh the environmental and health harms of making, running and discarding devices against the ways computing helps environmental work.
rows.evidence: The same machines also make environmental work possible

rows.reason: Students break a request into small pieces that each become a function, and describe the design in pseudocode with a branch and in charts the person who asked can check.
rows.evidence: One piece, one function

rows.reason: Students write and read files, handle the missing-file error their program is certain to meet, and decide what personal information a file should hold at all.
rows.evidence: Storing data about people is a decision, not a default

rows.reason: Students turn a formula into ordered, named arithmetic steps and check the program against one hand-worked example kept as a test case.
rows.evidence: Order the calculations so nothing is used before it exists.

rows.reason: Students learn why a syntax error stops a program before it starts while an error like a NameError appears only when the running program reaches that line.
rows.evidence: the translation failed before the work began

rows.reason: Students write a function so a repeated chunk lives in one place, name its parts, and work out what a call returns, including why a printing function returns None.
rows.evidence: A function is the fix: name a chunk of thinking once, then use the name.

rows.reason: Students read typed input into variables, convert it from text to the right type, and design the prompts and formatted output a user sees.
rows.evidence: always as text, never as a number

rows.reason: Students learn how malware and phishing get in and build a protection routine of updates, strong unique passwords with two-factor, and backups.
rows.evidence: Long, unique passwords in a password manager; two-factor on anything that matters

rows.reason: Students replace many separate variables with one list, index, insert and remove elements, and traverse a list to search it and find the highest value.
rows.evidence: Data that arrives together should live together.

rows.reason: Students draw a decision as a flow chart, write if/elif/else chains and nested ifs, and predict which branch runs, including one that can never be reached.
rows.evidence: In an `elif` chain, the most demanding condition goes first

rows.reason: Students write functions with parameters, defaults and return values, trace what each call produces, and build reusable small functions out of other functions.
rows.evidence: which is what modularity actually buys you

rows.reason: Students write counted and conditional loops, spot a loop that never ends, and use the accumulator pattern over a list as a reusable skeleton for totals, maximums and counts.
rows.evidence: the same skeleton finds a highest value, counts how many items match a condition

rows.reason: Students tell syntax, run-time and logic errors apart, find a bug by hand-tracing, and write a test plan of chosen inputs with expected results at the boundaries.
rows.evidence: A test plan is a table

rows.reason: Students follow the phases from problem definition to maintenance, build a thin end-to-end version first, and gather requirements by interviewing the person the program is for.
rows.evidence: Specifications come from people

rows.reason: Students name values in variables, read assignment as replacing a stored value, choose among int, float, str and bool, and see that every type is stored as bits.
rows.evidence: RAM holds nothing but binary

rows.reason: Students learn what a program is and name the input, processing and output of a small program before writing any code.
rows.evidence: Input: the minutes for each day. Process: add them up, divide by seven. Output: one sentence she can read on the bus.

rows.reason: Students look at how computing joined with other fields produces results neither field could reach alone.
rows.evidence: Pointed at another field's questions, it produces results neither could reach alone

rows.page: Concepts/Where to Take It, and Who to Ask
rows.reason: Students learn that a device given away with their files still on it exposes personal data, and how to erase it properly.
rows.evidence: A donated laptop with your files still on it is a privacy incident wearing a good deed's clothes.

rows.reason: Students index and slice strings, join them, and clean user input with built-in string methods rather than writing their own.
rows.evidence: A string is characters in order, indexed exactly like a list

rows.reason: Students discuss how a team that shares one background overlooks other people's problems, and what that does to who software serves.
rows.evidence: Whose problems get solved first when a team all share the same background

rows.reason: Students turn formulas into programs with well-named variables and arithmetic, then check results against a known input and output.
rows.evidence: Check it against a pair you know: 100 must give 212.

rows.reason: Students try unexpected inputs on a classmate's program, record what they expected against what happened, and hand over findings respectfully.
rows.evidence: What I typed | What I expected | What happened

rows.reason: Students interview a classmate about a repeated chore to pin down the real problem before any design begins.
rows.evidence: Read it back to them out loud. Watch their face. They will correct you

rows.reason: Students find patterns in forty daily counts to answer a real question, then discover that forty separate variables cannot be managed and a list is needed.
rows.evidence: forty separate names for forty related values is not merely tedious, it is unworkable

rows.reason: Students extend a sequential program by copying lines, hit a changed requirement, and are led to replace the copies with a loop.
rows.evidence: There has to be a way to just tell it to do that a hundred times.

rows.reason: Students predict the output of a grading if-chain, test a boundary mark after a change, and see how four copied blocks make changes error-prone compared with one named procedure.
rows.evidence: grade their change with a mark of exactly 71 in every position

rows.reason: Students write step-by-step instructions in plain language for a partner to follow literally, note where they failed, and revise them.
rows.evidence: Write a numbered list of instructions that gets your partner from six loose shapes to your exact figure.

rows.reason: Students trace which branch of an if/elif chain runs for each input, then extend it with a nested if and a condition joined with and.
rows.evidence: Exactly one of the four branches runs, and which one depends entirely on days_late

rows.reason: Students read and modify loops that validate input, total values, and track the largest value seen so far.
rows.evidence: accumulating: total_kilograms starts at zero and grows by one day's weight per pass

rows.reason: Students work with a program whose comments record a deliberate decision not to store borrowers' names, and loop over the saved lines to report and count them.
rows.evidence: The file holds TITLES and a number of days — never who borrowed what.

rows.reason: Students take typed input, see the run-time error a non-number causes and guard against it, and use integer division and remainder to format a result.
rows.evidence: ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'seven'

rows.reason: Students traverse a list of marks to total it, find the extremes and build a new list, in a program deliberately designed to hold no names.
rows.evidence: One list holds ten values under one name, so the program can ask questions of all of them at once.

rows.reason: Students write three small functions with parameters and return values, work out how a nested call is evaluated, and see why putting repeated arithmetic in one function makes later changes a one-place edit.
rows.evidence: this awkward little pair of lines now exists in exactly one place

rows.reason: Students run a program that executes top to bottom, storing changeable quantities in meaningfully named variables and computing results with arithmetic including // and %.
rows.evidence: Python starts at the top and runs one line at a time to the bottom

rows.reason: Students practise writing precise comments, journal entries and handover notes that explain what a program does for a reader who cannot ask them.
rows.evidence: Write for the next person, who might be you

rows.reason: On paper, students trace programs to state their exact output and find, classify and fix syntax, logic and run-time errors in short programs.
rows.evidence: Identify syntax, logic, and run-time errors, and say which is which

rows.reason: Students state the problem their app solves in the client's own words while the client runs it, and give classmates specific, respectful critique aimed at design decisions rather than people.
rows.evidence: attack the design question, never the designer

rows.reason: Students interview a real client to set requirements, build through dated milestones including a test with that user, and design the app to collect only the personal data it genuinely needs.
rows.evidence: Collect nothing you do not need

rows.reason: Students write a program that computes findings from a collected data set, clean up messy values, and turn the results into a recommendation while stating what the data cannot show.
rows.evidence: Data always arrives dirtier than promised

rows.reason: Students measure the energy cost of computers in a real space, weigh it against a way computing saves resources, and test their calculating program with a hand-worked case.
rows.evidence: One paragraph on the other side of the ledger

rows.reason: Students investigate one person's chore, sketch the conversation, and build a short script that takes that person's typed input and uses a conditional to give different advice.
rows.evidence: At least one decision: something the program handles differently depending on the answer

rows.reason: Students research a real computing project at the border with another field, explaining what problem it serves and what each field's expertise contributes to it.
rows.evidence: What the other field contributes, which is usually the part students skip

rows.reason: Students build a module of reusable functions, import it from a separate program, and document each function so a classmate can use the library from the notes alone.
rows.evidence: a classmate will import your toolbox and use it from your notes alone

rows.reason: Students organise a team project into finishable cards and milestones, including an early end-to-end skeleton, and report weekly on what is done, in progress and blocked.
rows.evidence: The walking-skeleton milestone is the one that saves projects

rows.reason: Students read a library function's reference entry to learn its parameters, defaults and return value, then call it on their own data to confirm its behaviour.
rows.evidence: What does it give back? A list of strings

rows.reason: Students adapt existing code shapes from documentation, snippets or their own earlier work, filling one placeholder at a time and running the program after each step.
rows.evidence: Run it after each `TODO` you close

rows.reason: Students locate a logic error with print statements and a debugger's breakpoints and stepping, and read a traceback to explain a run-time error.
rows.evidence: total = score replaces where it should add

rows.reason: Students learn a sequence of strategies for locating errors, from reading the message to printing values, halving the program, stepping through, and shrinking the failing input.
rows.evidence: You are printing to find the first place where the machine disagrees with you

rows.reason: Students build a test table of inputs with expected results decided in advance, choosing typical, boundary, empty and hostile cases.
rows.evidence: If the rule changes at 13, test 12 and 13

rows.reason: Students hand-trace a loop containing a conditional and a remainder test, recording each variable per pass to determine the printed result.
rows.evidence: One row per pass through the loop

dropped.why: The page explains operating systems, languages and applications as layers of software; CSP has no objective on system software, and the page gives students nothing to do that matches one.

The page is about the CPU, RAM, cache and storage and how they run a program; CSP has no objective on hardware components, and one line on a video card's parallel arithmetic is not enough to claim the parallel-computing objectives.
The page teaches reading hardware specifications and recommending a machine for a person's needs; no CSP learning objective covers choosing computer hardware.

The page is about identifying internal hardware components (memory, processor, cooling, data paths); no CSP learning objective covers computer architecture, and the network/device objectives do not fit.

The page has students choose hardware components and a budget for a client; CSP objectives on design and user investigation concern programs, not hardware purchasing, so nothing is defensible without stretching.

The page measures and multiplies device power use; environmental energy cost is not among the CSP learning objectives, and treating it as extracting information from data or as a beneficial/harmful effect would be a stretch.

The page is about matching hardware components and peripherals to a person's needs and budget; no CSP learning objective covers choosing computer hardware, and stretching the program-design objective to a purchase recommendation would not hold up.

Teaches keeping copies of your work in more than one place. The nearest objective, CSN-1.E, is about how the Internet's redundancy survives failures, not about a student's backups; claiming it would be a stretch.
